title: Celsus calls the creation story silly
source_text: Ἴδωμεν δὲ καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς, ἐν οἷς μιᾷ λέξει ἀποφηνάμενος καὶ μηδὲ κατὰ τὸ πιθανόν τι λέγων κατηγορεῖ τῆς κατὰ Μωϋσέα κοσμοποιΐας εἰπών· ἔτι γε μὴν καὶ ἡ κοσμογένεια μάλα εὐηθική. εἰ μὲν οὖν τὸν φαινόμενον αὐτῷ τρόπον τοῦ εὐηθικὴν εἶναι αὐτὴν καί τινας πιθανότητας προηνέγκατο, κἂν ἠγωνισάμεθα πρὸς αὐτάς· οὐκ εὔλογον δέ μοι φαίνεται πρὸς τὴν ἀπόφασιν αὐτοῦ κατασκευάσαι, τίνα τρόπον οὐκ ἔστιν εὐηθική. εἰ δέ τις βούλεται τὰ κινήσαντα ἡμᾶς καὶ μετὰ τῆς φανείσης ἀποδείξεως κατασκευασθέντα περὶ τῆς κατὰ Μωϋσέα κοσμοποιΐας θεω ρῆσαι, λαβέτω τὰ πραγματευθέντα ἡμῖν εἰς τὴν Γένεσιν ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρχῆς τοῦ βιβλίου μέχρι τοῦ „αὕτη ἡ βίβλος γενέσεως ἀνθρώπων,“ ἐν οἷς πεπειράμεθα ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν τῶν θείων γραμμάτων κατασκευάσαι, τίς ὁ „ἐν ἀρχῇ“ γενόμενος οὐρανὸς καὶ γῆ καὶ τὸ τῆς γῆς ἀόρατον καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστον, καὶ τίς ἡ ἄβυσσος καὶ τὸ ἐπ᾿ αὐτῆς σκότος, τί τε τὸ ὕδωρ καὶ τὸ ἐπιφερόμενον αὐτῷ „πνεῦμα τοῦ θεοῦ,“ καὶ τί τὸ γενητὸν „φῶς,“ τί τε „τὸ στερέωμα“ παρὰ τὸν „ἐν ἀρχῇ“ γενόμενον οὐρανὸν, καὶ οὕτω τὰ ἑξῆς. ἀπεφήνατο δὲ μάλα εὐηθικὴν εἶναι καὶ τὴν περὶ ἀνθρώπων γενέσεως γραφὴν, μήτε τιθεὶς τὰς δείξεις μήτ᾿ ἀγωνιζόμενος πρὸς αὐτάς· οὐ γὰρ εἶχεν οἶμαι λόγους ἀνατρέψαι δυναμένους τὸ „κατ᾿ εἰκόνα θεοῦ“ πεποιῆσθαι τὸν ἄνθρωπον. ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ συνίει τὸν ὑπὸ θεοῦ φυτευθέντα „παράδεισον“ καὶ τὴν προηγουμένην ἐν αὐτῷ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ζωὴν καὶ τὴν ἐκ περιστάσεως γενομένην, ἐκβληθέντος διὰ τὴν ἁμαρτίαν καὶ κατοικισθέντος ἐναντίον „τοῦ παραδείσου τῆς τρυφῆς.“ ὁ δὲ λέγων μάλα εὐηθικῶς ταῦτ᾿ εἰρῆσθαι πρῶτον ἐπιστησάτω καὶ ἑκάστῳ μὲν καὶ τῷδε· „ἔταξε τὰ χερουβὶμ καὶ τὴν φλογίνην ῥομφαίαν τὴν στρεφομένην, φυλάσσειν τὴν ὁδὸν τοῦ ξύλου τῆς ζωῆς.“ εἰ δ᾿ ἄρα μηδὲν νοήσας Μωϋσῆς ἀνέγραψε ταῦτα ἀλλὰ παραπλήσιόν τι ποιῶν οἷς παίζοντες οἱ τῆς ἀρχαίας κωμῳδίας ποιηταὶ ἀνεγράψαντο· Προῖτος ἔγημε Βελλεροφόντην, ὁ δὲ Πήγασος ἦν ἐξ Ἀρκαδίας· ἀλλ᾿ ἐκεῖνοι μὲν γελωτοποιεῖν θέλοντες τοιαῦτα συνέταττον, οὐ πιθανὸν δὲ τὸν ὅλῳ ἔθνει γραφὰς καταλιπόντα περὶ ὧν ἐβούλετο πεῖσαι τοὺς νομοθετουμένους ὅτι εἶεν ἐκ θεοῦ, ἀπρόσλογα γεγραφέναι καὶ χωρίς τινος νοῦ εἰρηκέναι τό· „ἔταξε τὰ χερουβὶμ καὶ τὴν φλογίνην ῥομφαίαν τὴν στρεφομένην, φυλάσσειν τὴν ὁδὸν τοῦ ξύλου τῆς ζωῆς“ ἢ ἄλλο τι τῶν περὶ τῆς ἀνθρώπων γενέσεως εἰρημένων καὶ ὑπὸ τῶν παρ᾿ Ἑβραίοις σοφῶν πεφιλοσοφημένων.
pass_a_gloss: Let us see also the next things, in which, declaring (ἀποφαίνομαι) in one phrase (λέξις) and saying nothing even according to the plausible (τὸ πιθανόν), he accuses (κατηγορέω) the world-making (κοσμοποιΐα) according to Moses, saying: 'Moreover also the world-genesis (κοσμογένεια) is very silly (εὐηθικός).' If then he had brought forward (προφέρω) the manner seeming to him of its being silly and some plausibilities (πιθανότητες), we would have contended against them; but it does not appear reasonable to me against his declaration (ἀπόφασις) to establish (κατασκευάζω) in what manner it is not silly. If anyone wishes to view (θεωρέω) the things that moved (κινέω) us and were established with the demonstration (ἀπόδειξις) that appeared (φαίνομαι) about the world-making according to Moses, let him take the things treated (πραγματεύομαι) by us on Genesis (Γένεσις) from the beginning of the book to 'this is the book of genesis of men', in which we have tried (πειράομαι) from the divine writings themselves to establish what the heaven and earth having come to be 'in the beginning' (ἐν ἀρχῇ) is, and the invisible (ἀόρατος) and unformed (ἀκατασκεύαστος) of the earth, and what the abyss (ἄβυσσος) and the darkness (σκότος) upon it, and what the water and the 'Spirit of God' borne upon (ἐπιφέρω) it, and what the made (γενητός) 'light', and what 'the firmament' (στερέωμα) beside the heaven having come to be 'in the beginning', and thus the next things. He declared very silly also the writing (γραφή) about the genesis of men, neither placing the proofs (δείξεις) nor contending against them; for he did not have, I think, arguments able to overturn (ἀνατρέπω) man having been made 'according to the image (εἰκών) of God'. But neither did he understand (συνίημι) the 'paradise' (παράδεισος) planted (φυτεύω) by God and the leading/original (προηγούμενος) life of man in it and the one having come to be from circumstance (ἐκ περιστάσεως), he being cast out (ἐκβάλλω) because of sin and settled (κατοικίζω) opposite 'the paradise of delight (τρυφή)'. The one saying these things to have been said very sillily, let him first attend to each and to this: 'he stationed (τάσσω) the cherubim and the flaming (φλόγινος) sword (ῥομφαία) turning (στρέφομαι), to guard the way of the tree (ξύλον) of life.' But if Moses, having understood (νοέω) nothing, wrote these, but doing something similar to what the poets of the ancient comedy (ἀρχαία κωμῳδία) jesting (παίζω) wrote: 'Proetus married (γαμέω) Bellerophon, and Pegasus was from Arcadia'; but those, wishing to make laughter (γελωτοποιέω), composed such things, while it is not plausible that the one having left behind writings to a whole nation (ἔθνος), about which he wished to persuade those legislated for (νομοθετέω) that they were from God, wrote irrelevant things (ἀπρόσλογα) and without some mind (νοῦς) said 'he stationed the cherubim ...' or anything else of the things said about the genesis of men and philosophized (φιλοσοφέω) by the wise among the Hebrews.
pass_b_english: Let us look also at what comes next, where he makes his pronouncement in a single phrase and, without saying anything even plausible, finds fault with Moses’ account of the making of the world, saying: “Moreover, the account of the world’s origin is also very silly.” Now if he had put forward the way in which it seemed to him silly, and some plausible arguments, we would have contended against them. But it does not seem reasonable to me to establish, in answer to his assertion, in what way it is not silly.

If anyone wishes to consider what moved us, and what we established, with what appeared to us a proof, about Moses’ account of the making of the world, let him take up what we have worked out on Genesis, from the beginning of the book as far as “This is the book of the generation of men” (Genesis 5:1). There we have tried, from the divine writings themselves, to establish what the heaven and earth are which came to be “in the beginning” (Genesis 1:1), and what is meant by the earth’s being invisible and unformed, and what the abyss is and the darkness upon it, and what the water is and the “Spirit of God” borne above it (Genesis 1:2), and what the “light” is which came to be (Genesis 1:3), and what “the firmament” is (Genesis 1:6) as distinct from the heaven made “in the beginning” (Genesis 1:1), and so on in order.

He has also pronounced the writing about the generation of human beings very silly, neither setting out the proofs nor contending against them. For he had, I think, no arguments able to overturn the statement that man was made “in the image of God” (Genesis 1:27). Nor did he understand the “paradise” planted by God (Genesis 2:8), and the life of man in it, which came first, and the life that came about through circumstance, when man was cast out because of sin and made to dwell opposite “the paradise of delight” (Genesis 3:24).

Let the man who says these things were told in a very silly way first attend to each of them, and to this one as well: “He stationed the cherubim and the flaming sword that turns, to guard the way of the tree of life” (Genesis 3:24). But suppose Moses wrote these things with no meaning in his mind, doing something like what the poets of the Old Comedy wrote in jest: “Proetus married Bellerophon, and Pegasus came from Arcadia.” Yet those poets put such things together because they wanted to raise a laugh; but it is not plausible that one who left writings to a whole nation, and wished to persuade those under his laws that these writings came from God, wrote what was irrelevant, and said without any meaning, “He stationed the cherubim and the flaming sword that turns, to guard the way of the tree of life” (Genesis 3:24), or any other of the things said about the generation of human beings and explored philosophically by the wise men among the Hebrews.

choices.choice: Celsus’s single phrase (ἔτι γε μὴν καὶ ἡ κοσμογένεια μάλα εὐηθική) is quoted; κοσμογένεια rendered ‘the account of the world’s origin’, εὐηθικός ‘silly’. ‘What we have worked out on Genesis’ refers to Origen’s Commentary on Genesis, now lost except for fragments. Genesis 5:1 in the Septuagint begins ‘This is the book of the generation of men’. ‘The earth’s being invisible and unformed’ follows the Septuagint of Genesis 1:2 (ἀόρατος καὶ ἀκατασκεύαστος); ‘Spirit of God’ is capitalised because Origen elsewhere reads it of the Holy Spirit. ‘The paradise of delight’ is the Septuagint of Genesis 3:24 (also 2:15 and 3:23). ‘Neither setting out the proofs nor contending against them’ (μήτε τιθεὶς τὰς δείξεις μήτ᾿ ἀγωνιζόμενος πρὸς αὐτάς) is ambiguous: the proofs may be Celsus’s own (for silliness) or those of Scripture; kept as open as the Greek. The sentence beginning ‘But suppose Moses wrote’ is broken in the Greek (εἰ δ᾿ ἄρα with no main clause before ἀλλ᾿ ἐκεῖνοι); rendered as a supposition answered by ‘Yet those poets’. The Old Comedy line about Proetus and Bellerophon is an unattributed fragment; no source cited. Source has θεω ρῆσαι split; read θεωρῆσαι.
'with a pronouncement in a single phrase' -> 'he makes his pronouncement in a single phrase' (μιᾷ λέξει ἀποφηνάμενος; smoother, same sense)
'against his bare assertion' -> 'in answer to his assertion' ('bare' was added to ἀπόφασις)

'writings he wished to persuade those receiving his laws had come from God' -> 'and wished to persuade those under his laws that these writings came from God' (περὶ ὧν ... ὅτι εἶεν ἐκ θεοῦ; broken English repaired)
Genesis 5:1, 1:1, 1:2, 1:3, 1:6, 1:27, 2:8 and 3:24 checked against the Septuagint wording quoted; correct
